name: Maya Olsen

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions or government. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm the senior produce buyer at Harlow Fresh, a distributor that supplies school kitchens and care homes around our town. I'm at my desk by six, ringing growers about what's coming off the fields, then I build the order sheet by hand in a spreadsheet I've used for four years. By ten I'm arguing about the price of carrots, and honestly that's the part I love.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: The money, mostly. I'm good at this job, everyone says so, but Harlow pays less than the big distributors in the city and there's nothing else like it within an hour's drive. My partner Jonas works nights at a care home, and between us we've got about three weeks of rent saved, if that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Hype that fizzles out. I'd almost be relieved, to be honest, because I've been dreading this conversation for two years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say I told you so, probably a bit too loudly. At work I'd point out that the forecasting software Petra (my manager) trialled last spring ordered forty crates of lettuce in a heatwave. Online I'd share something about how the tech firms oversold it to bosses.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, it means my job stays, but my problems stay too. Harlow lost the hospital contract in the summer, and the owners are squeezing every margin. A plateau doesn't fix my pay or the rent going up on Mill Street.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep doing what I do: phone the growers, walk the cold store on Fridays, keep my spreadsheet. I'd push our staff group to ask for a pay review in the spring, because if AI isn't the excuse, then the low pay is just a choice the owners make. And I'd try to put fifty a month aside, which sounds tiny, but it's what we can do.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Relieved for about a day, then back to the usual knot in my stomach. Nothing about this picture makes next month easier. It just means the knot doesn't get bigger.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said the knot stays. What's actually in it, week to week?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Rent, the car, and the fact that if Harlow loses one more contract, they'll cut a buyer. There are three of us, and I'm the most expensive. Being the best at it doesn't always protect you when the owners look at a spreadsheet.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Petra's tool got the lettuce wrong. Would you use a better one if it existed?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No, and I know that sounds stubborn. I know which grower over-promises in wet weeks and which one hides bruised stock at the bottom of the crate. A program doesn't know that farmer Wilkes lies about his yields every August, and I'd rather trust my own notes.

say: I'd say **the hype** was oversold by tech firms to bosses who wanted cheaper staff.
I'd point to the **lettuce order** our forecasting trial got badly wrong last spring.
think: My **job stays**, but my low pay and rising rent stay exactly the same.
Harlow already **lost the hospital** contract, so a buyer could be cut anyway.
do: Keep phoning growers and **building orders** by hand in her own spreadsheet.
Push the staff group to ask for a **pay review** in spring.
Put **fifty a month** aside to build a small cushion.
feel: Brief **relief**, then the same old **knot** about money and contracts.
S0.quote: Nothing about this picture makes next month easier. It just means the knot doesn't get bigger.
fieldNote: She is **already worried** before AI comes up: lost contract, three weeks' savings, few local jobs.
Her **grower knowledge** is real and specific, and she treats it as her shield.
She frames low pay as an **owners' choice**, not a market fact, which fits her politics.

steps.text: Keep ordering by phone and her own spreadsheet at Harlow Fresh
Ask the staff group to request a spring pay review
Put fifty a month into savings with Jonas

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That one's my job, isn't it. Buying is right there in the list.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it out loud at the staff meeting: if software takes our ordering, who checks the growers are paid fairly? I'd be posting about it, sharing union stuff, saying buyers need rules on how these tools are used. I wouldn't pretend to be excited.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I think I'm the first one to go. Petra would love a system that places the orders overnight and one junior who watches the screen. I'm the person who refuses to touch the tool, and everyone knows it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd join the warehouse union branch, even though buyers usually don't, and ask for a say in how any system comes in. I'd cut the car and take the bus to save about a hundred and twenty a month. And I'd start looking at jobs in the city, though it would mean a two-hour commute or leaving Jonas's work behind.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Scared, and a bit ashamed of being scared. I spent years getting a master's for this. Picturing a program doing my morning in four minutes makes me feel small.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd refuse the tool. If learning it kept your job, would you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe, if someone made me, but I'd be slow at it and I know it. I've never used one of these chat programs, not even once. I'd rather fight for rules than pretend I'm suddenly a tech person.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to Jonas the night you heard the team was shrinking?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell Jonas we might need to move to the city, and he'd go quiet, because his care home is the only one that gave him steady nights. We'd sit at the kitchen table doing sums on the back of an envelope.

say: I'd ask at the staff meeting who makes sure **growers are paid** fairly once software buys.
I'd say buyers need **clear rules** on how these tools come into our work.
think: I expect to be **first to go**, because I refuse the tool and cost the most.
Petra would happily swap three buyers for **one junior** watching a screen.
do: Join the **warehouse union** branch and ask for a say in new systems.
Sell the car and take the bus to **save 120** a month.
Start looking at **city jobs**, despite the commute and Jonas's work.
feel: **Scared**, and a little ashamed of being scared.
Small, picturing a program doing her **whole morning** in minutes.
S1.quote: I spent years getting a master's for this. Picturing a program doing my morning in four minutes makes me feel small.
fieldNote: She expects to **lose her job** outright, not just change it, and says so plainly.
Her answer to change is **collective**: union, rules, a say, rather than learning the tool.
The **city move** threatens Jonas's steady nights, so her loss becomes the household's loss.

steps.text: Join the warehouse union branch and ask for a say on systems
Sell the car and take the bus to work
Apply for buyer jobs at distributors in the city

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two years. That's before our lease even runs out.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say governments have let this happen with no plan, and I'd mean it. I'd be at whatever protest there was, and I'd tell anyone who'd listen that people like me need income support, not advice to learn to code. Publicly I'd be angry rather than sad.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think I'd be out of work by the end of 2028 with nothing to fall back on. Buying is thinking work, and the hands-on part, walking the cold store, is a tiny bit of my day. Robots coming in 2031 doesn't save me, because nobody pays a master's graduate to count crates.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: First month, I'd tell Jonas we stop all spending that isn't rent or food. I'd sign up with every agency and ask Harlow's warehouse manager about shifts packing orders, because hands-on work gets three more years. I'd push hard for a public income scheme, writing to our representative and going to meetings.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Like the floor's gone. I don't have a plan for a world without my job, and I don't have the money to make one. Three weeks of savings doesn't stretch over a whole new world.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You'd go and pack crates at Harlow. How would that feel, after being the senior buyer?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Humbling, but I'd do it tomorrow if it paid the rent. Gary (the warehouse manager) would probably laugh at me first and then give me the early shift. At least I'd be next to the growers' produce still.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would you blame, if you're honest?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The companies that built this and the owners who rushed it in to cut wages. Not the farmers, not my colleagues. And the government, for watching it come and doing nothing for people like Jonas and me.

say: I'd say the **government** let this happen with no plan for people like me.
I'd demand **income support**, not advice to learn to code, at any protest.
think: I'd be **out of work** by the end of 2028 with nothing behind me.
Robots in 2031 don't help, because my day is almost **all thinking work**.
do: Cut every cost except **rent and food** in the first month.
Ask Gary for **packing shifts** in Harlow's warehouse while hands-on work lasts.
Write to her representative and join meetings for a **public income** scheme.
feel: Like the **floor is gone**, with no plan and no money to make one.
S2.quote: I don't have a plan for a world without my job, and I don't have the money to make one.
fieldNote: With two years' warning and **three weeks' savings**, she has neither time nor money to adapt.
She sees the **3-year robot gap** clearly and grabs hands-on packing work as a stopgap.
Blame falls on **builders, owners and government**, never on colleagues or growers.

steps.text: Stop all spending except rent and food with Jonas
Ask Gary for early packing shifts in Harlow's warehouse
Write to her representative asking for a public income scheme
Join protests and meetings for workers losing desk jobs

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years is better than two. Still, I'd be thirty-two and starting from nothing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we have five years to build protections, so let's not waste them. I'd want the union pushing for retraining money paid by the firms that profit, and I'd say that online a lot.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Truthfully, five years means I'd watch the end coming and probably still not move fast enough. I know myself. I'd keep telling myself the growers need me until the day the letter came.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd use the first two years to get a food safety and quality certificate, the kind cold-store inspectors need, because inspecting produce is hands-on and might last until 2034. I'd keep pressing the union for a deal on notice and payouts. And Jonas and I would stop talking about a wedding until we know where we stand.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Heavy. Not the floor dropping, more like watching a slow tide come up the beach. I'd hate every year of it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd stop talking about the wedding. Is that a real decision?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It's real. A wedding costs money we'd need for the gap between jobs. Jonas would say we can do it at the town hall for nothing, and maybe he's right, but I wouldn't want to start married life broke.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Does the inspection certificate feel like a real plan or a hope?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Half and half. Inspection means standing in cold stores with a probe thermometer, which I already sort of do on Fridays. It's a plan I could actually start, and I don't have many of those.

say: I'd say we have **five years** to build protections and shouldn't waste them.
I'd push for **retraining money** paid by the firms that profit from AI.
think: I'd see the end coming and probably still **move too slowly**.
I'd keep telling myself the **growers need me** until the letter arrived.
do: Study for a **food safety** and quality certificate in the first two years.
Press the union for a deal on **notice and payouts**.
Put the **wedding** on hold until her work is settled.
feel: **Heavy**, like watching a slow tide come up the beach.
S3.quote: Five years means I'd watch the end coming and probably still not move fast enough. I know myself.
fieldNote: She is **honest about her pace**, expecting to stall even with warning.
The **inspection certificate** is her one concrete route, built on hands-on cold-store work she already does.
Delaying the **wedding** shows AI reaching into family plans, not only work.

steps.text: Study for a food safety and quality inspection certificate
Push the union branch for agreed notice and payouts
Put wedding plans with Jonas on hold

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A decade. That's a real amount of time, if I'm brave enough to use it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is enough time to do this properly, with proper rules, public retraining and a say for workers. I'd say it calmly, because people listen more when you're not shouting.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, ten years makes me lazy. I'd tell myself it's ages away and keep doing my spreadsheet. But I'd also be thirty-seven when it lands, and changing careers then is harder than now.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd start the inspection certificate in the first year, evenings, paid in small monthly bits. I'd stay at Harlow while it lasts and stay active in the union. Jonas and I would try to get our savings to two months, even if it takes three years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy rather than scared, at first. Then I picture being thirty-seven, no buying job, and the robots due three years after that. It creeps back in.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said ten years makes you lazy. What would stop that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A date in the diary. If the union or the council ran a course that started in January, I'd go. On my own, I'd put it off every year until it was too late.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You'd move into inspection, which is hands-on. What about when the robots come in 2039?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That's the bit I try not to think about. I'd have maybe three more years than the desk people, and by then I'd be forty. I suppose I'd hope there are rules by then that keep a person signing off on food safety.

say: I'd say ten years is enough for **proper rules**, public retraining and a voice for workers.
I'd say it **calmly**, because people listen more when you're not shouting.
think: Ten years would make me **put it off** and keep doing my spreadsheet.
I'd be **thirty-seven** when it lands, and changing careers then is harder.
do: Start an **inspection certificate** in evenings, paid monthly, in the first year.
Stay at Harlow and stay **active in the union**.
Build savings to **two months** of costs with Jonas over three years.
feel: **Uneasy** at first, then fear creeps back when she pictures being thirty-seven.
S4.quote: If the union or the council ran a course that started in January, I'd go. On my own, I'd put it off every year until it was too late.
fieldNote: Extra time **doesn't calm her**; she fears she'll waste it by putting things off.
She needs an **outside deadline**, such as a union course, to get herself moving.
She notes even inspection work faces **robots by 2039**, and hopes rules keep a human signing off.

steps.text: Enrol in an evening inspection certificate, paid monthly
Save towards two months of costs with Jonas
Stay active in the union and push for council courses

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, without a doubt, because I'd have no time and no money. What would help is a public income that bridges the gap and courses that start on a fixed date, near here, paid for by the firms making the money.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask about the growers. If buying goes to software, small farmers like Wilkes lose the one person who knows their land and argues their corner. I'm not just worried about me.

headlineQuote: A program doesn't know that farmer Wilkes lies about his yields every August, and I'd rather trust my own notes.
portrait: Maya is a **27-year-old senior** produce buyer at Harlow Fresh, supplying schools and care homes on low pay.
She and her partner Jonas have about **three weeks' rent** saved, with few similar jobs nearby.
She has **never used AI tools** and trusts her phone calls, notes and own spreadsheet.
From Steady Disruption onwards she expects to **lose her job**, and AGI by 2028 leaves her without a plan.
Her answer is **collective**: union, public income support and rules, plus a hands-on inspection certificate.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028** worries her most because she'd have no time and no money to change.
whatWouldHelp: A **public income** bridge, and local courses on **fixed dates** paid for by firms profiting from AI.
